html:
Surah Al-Wāqiʿah (The Inevitable Event) is the 56th surah of the Qur’an — ninety-six verses revealed in Makkah. Its name comes from the opening verse: “When the Inevitable Event comes to pass, no one will deny its coming.” The whole surah is a vivid pre-view of the Day of Judgment: the splitting of the earth and sky, the raising of mankind into three distinct ranks — the Foremost (al-Sābiqūn), the Companions of the Right (Aṣḥāb al-Yamīn), and the Companions of the Left (Aṣḥāb al-Shimāl) — and the recompense awaiting each. Classical mufassirūn from Ibn Kathīr onward read it as a Makkī surah whose purpose is to detach the heart from the illusions of this world by making the next world almost touchable. The repeated rhetorical refrain, “Then which of your Lord’s favours will you deny?”-echoing Al-Rahmān, places the human being between gratitude and ruin.

Al-Wāqiʿah is popularly called the Sūrat al-Ghinā — the Surah of Wealth — on the strength of a narration from Ibn Masʿūd: “Whoever recites Surah al-Wāqiʿah every night will never be afflicted by poverty.” This hadith is recorded in al-Bayhaqī’s Shuʿab al-Īmān 2267-2270 and Mishkāt al-Maṣābīḥ 2181. The chain contains Shujāʿ ibn al-Walīd and Abū Fāṭimah, and al-Albānī graded it daʿīf (weak) in al-Silsilah al-Daʿīfah no. 289 — the final word of al-Bayhaqī himself on the chain was that it is weak. A separate chain via Abū Yaʿlā was called jayyid (good) by al-Zaylaʿī in Takhrīj al-Kashshāf, which is why many scholars — Imam al-Nawawī in al-Adhkār, Ibn al-Ḥājj in al-Madkhal, Mullā ʿAlī al-Qārī — continued to narrate it. The honest position is the one shared by Ibn Masʿūd’s own biographers and by Shaykh al-Albānī: the chains are weak but the practice itself is virtuous because it is reciting the Qur’an, and the reward of recitation is already established in Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 2910 (hasan sahih): ten good deeds for every letter of the Qur’an. The surah does not need a special-case bonus to be worth your nightly time.

What is firmly established is that the Prophet ﷺ himself gave Al-Wāqiʿah a specific place in his routine. Jābir ibn Samurah narrated: “The Messenger of Allah used to recite Al-Wāqiʿah and surahs like it in the Fajr prayer” — reported by Imām Aḥmad in his Musnad and corroborated by multiple chains in Sunan an-Nasā’ī and Sahih Muslim’s descriptions of the Prophet’s Fajr recitation. In another well-known report, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq ﷺ said to the Prophet, “O Messenger of Allah, you have aged.” The Prophet replied, “Surah Hūd, al-Wāqiʿah, al-Mursalāt, ʿAmma Yatasā’alūn, and Idhā al-Shamsu Kuwwirat have aged me” — recorded in Jāmiʿ at-Tirmidhī 3297 (hasan gharīb). Each of those five surahs confronts the believer with the Day of Standing. Al-Wāqiʿah earns its place among them because it does not just mention Judgment — it stages it, scene by scene, until the reader can almost hear the trumpet.

Ibn Kathīr’s structural reading of the surah frames it as a courtroom in three acts. First the cosmic shaking (verses 1-6): mountains crumbled to dust, mankind sorted. Then the three groups set out in detail (vv. 7-56): the Foremost at the summit, the Companions of the Right in gardens of ease, the Companions of the Left in scorching wind and poisoned shade. Finally the proof-section (vv. 57-96): six evidences — human conception, agriculture, water, fire, the stars, and the Qur’an itself — each ending with a demand for gratitude. Reading it nightly is less about repelling poverty and more about repelling heedlessness; the surah refuses to let the reader go to sleep forgetting that this world is a borrowed thing. That, more than any virtue narration, is why the Ṣaḥābah loved it.
